title: Al-Kahf, part two
tomorrow: a whole surah named for a woman. was she a prophet?

lines: A HOLE IN A POOR FAMILY'S BOAT.
cards: Some coaches make a call that looks plain wrong, and it only makes sense weeks later. The second half of al-Kahf runs on that feeling.
Musa sets out to find a servant of God who knows what he doesn't, and asks to follow him and learn. The man warns him he won't have the patience. Musa promises he will.
They step onto a boat, and the man quietly breaks a hole in it. A boat that belongs to poor people. Why would anyone wise do that?

teach.b: Musa can't keep quiet. Have you holed it to drown its people? Then a second act, the hardest in the story, involving a boy, and Musa objects again.
Then a third: in a town that refused them food, the man rebuilds a falling wall and asks no wage. Musa says he could at least have been paid.
Three strikes, and they part, but first the reasons. A king ahead was seizing every sound boat by force; a damaged one would be passed over and stay with its poor owners.

The wall stood over the treasure of two orphan boys whose father was righteous, kept until they were grown. And the boy's parents, the surah says, were believers, and their Lord would give them better.
Then the man says, in Pickthall's words: "I did it not upon my own command."
Here's the part to tell a friend: the Qur'an never names him. It calls him one of Our servants; the name al-Khidr comes from the hadith. The surah ends its journeys with a builder too.
Dhul-Qarnayn, a traveler with power, raises a barrier to protect a people, refuses their payment, and says: "This is a mercy from my Lord."
Both men did hard, odd things that turned out to be mercy. Musa was told the reasons. The surah never promises everyone the same.
The puzzle's answer isn't that every loss is secretly good. It's that mercy can work out of sight.

how: The journey of Musa and al-Khidr is sometimes retold when someone is facing a loss they can't make sense of, and the story is read in full as part of al-Kahf on Fridays.

o: a surah of laws on trade and fair contracts
the Cave: the surah of journeys and hidden mercy
the Spider, about houses too weak to hold

games.q: the act and the reason — tap the pairs.
p: a king was seizing every sound boat

s: the Qur'an names the man Musa traveled with
it calls him one of Our servants. the name al-Khidr comes from the hadith.
the boat was damaged to protect its poor owners
a king ahead was taking every sound boat; a damaged one was passed over.
the story promises you'll always learn the reason for a loss
Musa was told the reasons. the surah's point is that mercy can work out of sight.

games.q: your little brother hears the story and asks why the wise man broke a poor family's boat. what's the honest short answer?
o: a king was seizing good boats; a damaged one would be left to them.
to teach the poor family not to love their things too much.
just to test whether Musa could keep quiet, nothing more.
games.why: the surah gives the reason itself (18:79): the damage kept the boat out of a king's hands, so its owners kept their living.

practice: Take a pen and write one line by hand: something in your life right now that looks like a hole in the boat. Under it, leave a blank line. Don't fill it in.
Sit with the blank, the way Musa had to before the reasons came.

wordCard.voice: Al-Kahf, its second half: a teacher whose damage hid mercy, and a builder who called his wall a mercy from his Lord.

orig.note: Arabic: mercy. the word behind Dhul-Qarnayn's line, a mercy from my Lord.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: hidden mercy, even when the reason comes late, or not at all. Al-Kahf, read through.
